title: The org chart nobody has seen
setting: Two directors prepare an answer for the board before December.

lines.t: The board of directors wants an answer before December.
Which answer? The merger, or the restructure?
Both are on the table. The acquisition would give us 9% market share overnight.
And two headquarters, four hundred kilometres apart.
That's the part nobody ever costs properly.
Have you drawn the new org chart?
Twice. Both versions have people reporting to two managers.
Then it isn't finished. What do we tell the stakeholders?
That we're looking at growth, which is true, and that nobody is being downsized, which I hope is true.
Leave the second one out. Our competitive advantage is that people stay here nine years. Say what you know, and say when you'll know the rest.

title: Four months in
setting: HR and the operations director go through the people decisions due this month.

lines.t: Nadya's probation period ends on the 30th.
Her line manager says she's the best hire this year.
Then write it in the performance review, because she'll read it.
What about the job description? She's doing more than it says.
Rewrite it now, before somebody argues about pay later.
And the headcount for next year?
Two more, if the budget holds. One of them should be a direct report for Kiril.
Kiril has eleven. That's a queue, not a team.
Which brings us to succession planning, because he's the only person who knows the Varna contracts.
Then fix the onboarding for the next two. Last year we paid severance to somebody we should have promoted, and I'd rather not repeat that.

title: In house or not
setting: A director and a project lead decide what the company should stop doing itself.

lines.t: Procurement wants to run a tender for the cleaning contract.
For cleaning? That's three months of paperwork.
It's the rule above forty thousand.
Fine. And the software support, do we outsource that too?
That one I'd keep in house.
Because of cost?
Because of speed. A vendor with a service level agreement answers in four hours. Our own person answers in four minutes.
Four minutes when he's here.
Which is the honest argument against me, and it's why we're having this conversation.
Write both options down with real numbers. Let the tender settle the cleaning while we argue about the software.

title: Two more small things
setting: A client keeps adding requests that are each too small to refuse.

lines.t: The client has asked for two more small things.
How small?
Two days each. That's the fourth 'small thing' this month.
Then it's scope creep and we name it out loud.
The scope was agreed in March.
Go back to the business case. If the extras serve the same goal, price them and move a milestone. If they don't, they wait.
They don't. They're somebody's personal preference.
Then say so politely and show them the roadmap.
And the deliverable for the 30th?
Unchanged. Two small things do not move a date that eleven people are planning around.

title: Against what
setting: Sales are down and the board will want a reason.

lines.t: Sales are down 6% on last year.
Against what benchmark?
Against our own target, which we set in a very good month.
And against the market?
The market is down 11%.
So the market is having a worse year than we are, and the target was the optimistic part.
The board will still ask why we missed it.
Then show both numbers on the same page. One KPI with nothing to compare it to tells nobody anything.
And next year's target?
Set it against what the market actually does. Our best quarter ever is a bad place to start from, and anyone measured that way underperforms on paper.

title: Getting buy-in
setting: Two managers discuss a restructure before presenting it.

lines.t: Before we take this to the board, we need buy-in from the regional heads.
All four of them? Two will push back hard.
Probably. What's their main objection?
Headcount. They think restructuring is a word for cutting jobs.
It isn't, and we should say that in plain language at the town hall.
Then we need numbers. How many roles actually change?
Eleven people get a new line manager. Nobody is made redundant.
Say exactly that. Vague answers are what start the rumours.
Agreed. I'll put it on one slide and take questions for as long as they last.
Good. And get sign-off from HR before Thursday.

title: Nobody reads it
setting: Planning the company meeting, and what people will really turn up for.

lines.t: The town hall is on the 12th. Do you want the mission statement on the first slide?
Does anybody read it?
Honestly, no. People quote the coffee machine rule far more often.
Then that's the corporate culture. The real one.
The agenda has hybrid work on it. That's what they'll come for.
Then put it first and give it twenty minutes.
I need sign-off from you before the agenda goes out.
You have it. Who's taking the minutes?
Nadya. And if anyone asks something we can't answer, I'll escalate it and reply within the week.
Say that out loud in the room. One honest 'I don't know yet' buys more buy-in than a slide with our values on it.

title: The counteroffer
setting: A supplier responds to a client's much lower offer.

lines.t: We've reviewed your quote. Our counteroffer is 38% lower.
That's a big gap. Can I ask what's driving the number?
Procurement has a fixed budget for this category.
Understood. At that price I'd be taking teachers off profitable work.
So it's a no?
It's a different yes. Three locations instead of nine, at our rate.
A pilot, effectively.
Exactly. With an option to extend if the results hold.
I'll take that back to the team. It might get through faster, actually.
Take your time. The offer stands until the end of the quarter.

title: The number you'd walk away at
setting: A price has come back lower than asked and a counteroffer is due.

lines.t: They came back at eighteen. We asked twenty-two.
What's your counteroffer?
Twenty-one, with the training included.
Before you send it, tell me the number you'd walk away at.
Nineteen.
Then say nineteen out loud now, to me, so you don't discover it at half past six on a Friday.
What's our leverage?
They've told two of their own clients we start in April. That's leverage, and it disappears the day they sign with somebody else.
So do I push, or do I close the deal?
Negotiate the training, hold the price, and give them something they can announce. A win-win that both sides can explain internally closes faster than a better number.
